newsitem.title: CANADA: Negotiators battle to end GM Canada strike with deal.
newsitem.headline: Negotiators battle to end GM Canada strike with deal.

text.p: Negotiators for General Motors Corp. and the Canadian Auto Workers union said Sunday they were bargaining hard to find a labor agreement to end a strike of 26,000 workers in Canada before it entered its third week.
CAW president, Buzz Hargrove, said he believed it was difficult, but possible to reach a settlement with the world's largest automaker by a Monday noon deadline.
"I went from much less optimistic this morning to cautiously optimistic, but boy you'd have to be really reached to think we can do this," Hargrove told Reuters.
GM Canada spokesman, Stew Low told Reuters that the two sides had exchanged contractual language on outsourcing and the possible sale of two plants in Canada.
"There is a lot of language being exchanged actually defining terms and conditions," he said.
However, both sides cautioned there was a lot of work to complete to fashion an agreement by the Monday noon (4:00 p.m. GMT) deadline the two sides had set on Wednesday.
"We just haven't done a lot of work yet," Hargrove said. Unless (they've) got offer one, two and three sitting there then it's going to be tough."
The two sides returned to the bargaining table on Friday afternoon, after making little progress since the strike began more than two weeks ago.

Talks between the two sides have produced little results since the strike began around midnight Oct 2. after GM refused to agree to the outsourcing limits laid out in the pattern contract reached by Chrysler and the CAW in September.

General Motors said before bargaining began at the Big Three North American automakers in August that it intended to sell at least two of its parts plants in Canada and contract out jobs at other plants for a total job loss to the CAW of about 5,500.
Hargrove has continued to say he will reverse those decisions and hammer out a deal on the practice of contracting out work to non-union companies, known as outsourcing.

In September, the union signed a pattern agreement with Chrysler Corp., which banned the sale or closure of any plants over the next three years and committed Chrysler to replacing any jobs lost to outsourcing in Canada.
Traditionally, the union sets the pattern for all three companies at its first negotiating target and the others follow, but this year General Motors balked at the scope of the Chrysler pattern.

The stalemate in talks ended on Wednesday after General Motors Chairman Jack Smith flew to Toronto to meet with Hargrove and agreed to accept limits on the automaker's outsourcing decisions in order to end a sit-in occupation of one of the two plants up for sale.

If an agreement is ratified, the workers could be back at work at GM plants across Canada by next week and the union will begin labor talks with Ford Motor Co., the last of the Big Three automakers in Canada.
The strike has paralyzed GM plants throughout Canada and has idled 7,478 auto workers in the United States and Mexico, with more plant shutdowns possible if it continues this week.
